topics.topic: How admission verdicts are deterministic when implementations can access time or randomness
questions: Is an AdmissionVerdict a deterministic fact of the implementation and corpus, or may it permanently be whichever verdict resulted from the first admission execution of code whose undetected time or randomness changes its outputs?
What does “deterministic verdict” mean when the admitted implementation may obtain time or randomness through an undetected route and therefore produce different outputs for the same trial case?
For an implementation whose trial outputs can vary with time or chance, what fact makes its admission verdict deterministic for a fixed implementation and corpus?

quotes:
2. Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs
   admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the
   current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used. The
   corpus digest is the content identity (State 6, decision 14) of the list of
   its `trial_case_id`s in corpus order.
   Admission executes the implementation on every case of the corpus, in corpus
   order, each as one TrialExecution M07, and never stops early — save for an
   execution whose cleanup cannot be confirmed: it is recorded `crashed` with
   `cleanup_failed` and the kernel stops (A03 rule 7), with no verdict
   recorded; after the restart a submission runs admission afresh.

3. A case passes when the execution succeeded and, if the case states expected
   outputs, every output's digest equals the expected one — a file output is
   recorded in the TrialExecution by digest, size and media type, keeps no bytes,
   and is compared with the expected file fixture by digest; a `many` file output
   equals its expected list when both have the same length and the digests are
   equal position by position, so order and repetitions count; outputs that
   validate but differ are `output_mismatch`. The verdict is `admitted` exactly
   when the corpus is non-empty and every case passed; otherwise `refused` with
   reason `empty_corpus`, or with the first case in corpus order that did not
   pass and its outcome.
judgement.why: State 2 decides that the first admission executes the corpus and records the verdict determined by those observed executions, while later submissions of the same implementation and corpus digest reuse that recorded verdict.

topics.topic: Whether unchanged resubmissions reuse the existing admission verdict and evidence or rerun the corpus
questions: When an existing implementation is submitted again against the same corpus digest, must the kernel reuse the recorded verdict and its original TrialExecutions, or rerun every case and compute new admission evidence?

When an equal implementation is submitted again while the corpus digest is unchanged, does the kernel reuse the existing AdmissionVerdict and its TrialExecutions, or run the corpus again and create fresh admission evidence?

When the same implementation is submitted again while the corpus digest is unchanged, does admission create new TrialExecution records, or does it return the recorded verdict without running the cases?

quotes:
The one verdict on one implementation over the whole active corpus of its
contract version (K-05): recorded once and then reused, never computed again
(A04 rule 2).

Computed by the kernel when an implementation is submitted, from the
TrialExecutions of that admission: every active
case of the corpus is run again for the implementation at admission time, and the
verdict covers exactly those executions.
judgement.divergence: An equal resubmission either reuses the existing verdict without executing cases, or reruns every case and creates fresh TrialExecutions; the submitting agent inspecting admission and trial evidence notices the difference.
judgement.why: One passage requires permanent reuse of the recorded verdict, while the other says every active case is run again when the implementation is submitted.

topics.topic: Whether implementation purity is required or merely approximated by blocking known time and randomness APIs
questions: Is independence from time and chance a required fact of every function implementation, or is it only enforced by blocking the standard-library entry points while other time- or chance-dependent code remains eligible for trial and admission?

judgement.why: This asks the same question as P1 about whether undetected time- or chance-dependent code is refused for impurity or judged by its observed outputs, and the passage deciding it has not changed.

precedent.topic: Whether purity is an admission requirement beyond blocking named capabilities
quotes:
The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.
precedent.why: The changed passage expressly says alternate time or chance access is not detected and the code is judged by its observed outputs, so passing such code is not refused merely for that undetected dependency.
